background.speaker: SPEAKER_01
background.text: It's great to have somebody who's both practiced in private practice, now back in private practice, and also has been in the government for a good long stint. Because when your general counsel, which I was for a couple of years some time ago, it's a challenge to know how to deal with the government when you have legal issues come up. So let's talk about what that experience is and what it should be. You can help us from both sides, but particularly from the federal law enforcement agency side, because a lot of us, certainly I never practiced in the federal law enforcement agency. I don't know that experience. And let's take an example just from the headlines today. We have Danska Bank, which has this money laundering thing through a European country, like $250 billion, most of which they say now is questionable. And we knew that. The CEO stepped down. But now today we learned the federal law enforcement agency has sort of called them up and said, we're kind of interested in that. Why don't you tell us about that? We're going to investigate it. Give us a sense of, first of all, from the federal law enforcement agency's point of view, how does the agency find out about that? Are they reading the Financial Times? Are they reading the Wall Street Journal and saying, wait a second, what's going on? How likely would they discover something like that?

ground_truth: Well, first, I recognize it can be a scary and mysterious thing when you hear from the government. And certainly for folks on the outside, whether you're in-house counsel or private counsel, I know there oftentimes it's like there's this cloak of secrecy around how the federal agency is approaching these things and what the thinking is behind that. First, in terms of how the department gets matters that are investigated, it comes from the full gamut of things. It could be in the financial industry from suspicious activity reports or other reporting from a financial institution itself or a corresponding financial institution. It could be from someone inside who views themselves as a whistleblower, may then come either to the federal agency or other regulatory bodies to alert the government. Sometimes it can be from clients or those who are participating in financial transactions. It's really a wide variety of sources then, and then the department has to sift through that information and try to make a determination as to what is really worthy of the department's attention.
bio:
The subject (born 1960) is an American lawyer. They served as a federal prosecutor, later Deputy Head of a federal law enforcement agency, having been appointed to both positions by the president, and later was Acting Head of the same agency.

Following the inauguration of a new president and the departure of the previous agency head on January 20, 2017, they served as Acting Head for 10 days. They were dismissed for insubordination on January 30, after instructing the agency not to make legal arguments defending an executive order, which temporarily banned the admission of refugees and barred travel from certain countries on the grounds that terrorists were using the refugee resettlement program to enter the country.

Rather than defend it, they stated the order was neither defensible in court nor consistent with the Constitution. The speaker's MBTI type is ESFJ
